Chapter 6: Reclaiming Agency—Restoring Control and Choice
When you think about trauma, one of the deepest wounds it leaves behind is that sense of losing control. Maybe you’ve felt it—the way your mind and body just get swept up in something overwhelming, and suddenly, nothing feels like it’s up to you anymore. Healing starts, in many ways, with gently reclaiming that sense of agency. It’s about building back the quiet confidence that says, “I can shape my own experience. I get to make choices, and respond to life’s challenges.”
Now, this process doesn’t begin with some huge, dramatic moment. More often, it starts with the little things. Imagine someone who’s felt powerless for a long time. For them, even deciding what to eat for breakfast, or choosing how to spend the afternoon, can be a meaningful act of self-direction. These everyday choices may seem simple, but they send a powerful message to the nervous system: “I have a say in what happens to me now.”
Another important piece is learning to tune back into your body’s signals. After trauma, things like hunger, tiredness, or even pleasure can feel confusing—or sometimes, just plain unsafe. Gentle practices, like mindful eating, doing a body scan, or even taking a moment to notice how you’re feeling, help rebuild trust with your body. And over time, your body stops being a source of fear and starts to become a partner in healing.
So, what are some practical ways to support this return of agency?
First, let’s talk about choice in therapy. When someone gets to set the pace, pick which topics feel right, or even decide to skip an exercise, it sends a clear message: their voice matters, and they’re in control.
Then there’s skill-building. Learning new ways to cope—like grounding techniques, assertive communication, or relaxation skills—can really open up what feels possible.
And don’t forget to celebrate small wins. Noticing and honoring even tiny moments of self-advocacy, like speaking up for yourself or making a decision, helps build trust in your own capacity.
Let me give you a real-world example. Picture someone who’s avoided social gatherings for years. One day, they choose to attend a small get-together. It might be tough to be there—but the important thing is, they made the choice to go. And if it gets overwhelming, leaving early is also their decision. That simple act of choosing is a powerful step toward reclaiming autonomy.
Agency isn’t about never feeling vulnerable, or trying to control everything. It’s about knowing that—even when life is uncertain—you have tools, and you have choices. That shift, right there, is the foundation for deeper healing, and for building a life that truly feels your own.
